'use strict'

/**
 * Value certification module. Certifies that parameters passed to ranged-date
 * are of expected types and ranges.
 *
 * @private
 * @module cert-is
 * @external
 * @see {@link https://github.com/jpcx/cert-is}
 */
const cert = require('cert-is')

/**
 * Returns true only if value falls within range.
 *
 * @private
 * @param {number} t - Number being tested.
 * @param {number} l - Lower bound.
 * @param {number} u - Upper bound.
 * @returns {boolean} True if number falls within range, false if not.
 * @example
 * // returns true
 * inRange(0, -1, 1)
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * inRange(-1, 0, 1)
 */
const inRange = (t, l, u) => t > l && t < u
/**
 * Returns the difference of a number and the current date in ms as years from the current date.
 *
 * @private
 * @param {number} target - Number to subtract from.
 * @returns {number} Years until given time in ms.
 * @example
 * // returns years until unix epoch
 * yrDist(0)
 * @example
 * // returns 1
 * yrDist(Date.now() + 31536000000)
 */
const yrDist = target => (target - Date.now()) / +'31536e6'
/**
 * Returns the given number only if it falls within a given range in years from the current date.
 *
 * @private
 * @param {number} target - Number being tested.
 * @param {number} yrBack   - Years before current date as lower bound.
 * @param {number} yrFwd    - Years after current date as upper bound.
 * @returns {(number|boolean)} Number falls within range.
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * bound(Date.now(), 5, 5)
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * bound(Date.now() * 1000, 5, 5)
 */
const bound = (target, yrBack, yrFwd) =>
  inRange(yrDist(target), -yrBack, yrFwd) && target
/**
 * Returns time in ms if number itself, seconds equivalent, or microseconds equivalent falls within a given range in years from the current date.
 *
 * @private
 * @param   {number}  target     - Number being tested.
 * @param   {number}  yrBack     - Years before current date as lower bound.
 * @param   {number}  yrFwd      - Years after current date as upper bound.
 * @param   {Object}  exclusions - Specifies interpretation exclusions, if any.
 * @param   {boolean} [exclusions.us=false] - Exclude microseconds interpretation.
 * @param   {boolean} [exclusions.ms=false] - Exclude milliseconds interpretation.
 * @param   {boolean} [exclusions.s=false]  - Exclude seconds interpretation.
 * @returns {(number|boolean)}  Converted ms or false if outside range.
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * check(Date.now(), 5, 5, {})
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * check(Date.now() / 1000, 5, 5, {})
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * check(Date.now() * 1000, 5, 5, {})
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * check(Date.now() - 100000000000, 5, 5, {})
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms - 100000000000
 * check(Date.now() - 100000000000, 5, 5, {})
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * check(Date.now(), 5, 5, { ms: true })
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * check(Date.now(), 5, 5, { s: true, us: true })
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * check(Date.now() / 1000, 5, 5, { s: true })
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * check(Date.now() / 1000, 5, 5, { ms: true, us: true })
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * check(Date.now() * 1000, 5, 5, { us: true })
 * @example
 * // returns current time in ms
 * check(Date.now() * 1000, 5, 5, { ms: true, s: true })
 * @example
 * // returns false
 * check(Date.now(), 5, 5, { ms: true, s: true , us: true })
 */
const check = (target, yrBack, yrFwd, exclusions) =>
  isFinite(target) &&
  ((!exclusions.ms && bound(target, yrBack, yrFwd)) ||
    (!exclusions.s && bound(target * 1000, yrBack, yrFwd)) ||
    (!exclusions.us && bound(target / 1000, yrBack, yrFwd)))

/**
 * Converts a given string, number, or Date object to the number of milliseconds since the Unix epoch, provided that it can be recognized as millisecond, second, or microsecond time within a specified range from the current date.
 *
 * @public
 * @module ranged-date
 * @param {(Date|number|string)} data - Data to attempt to recognize as valid date.
 * @param   {number}  yrBack     - Years before current date as lower bound.
 * @param   {number}  yrFwd      - Years after current date as upper bound.
 * @param   {Object}  exclusions - Specifies interpretation exclusions, if any.
 * @param   {boolean} [exclusions.us=false] - Exclude microseconds interpretation.
 * @param   {boolean} [exclusions.ms=false] - Exclude milliseconds interpretation.
 * @param   {boolean} [exclusions.s=false]  - Exclude seconds interpretation.
 * @returns {(number|boolean)} Converted time in ms or false if outside range.
 * @throws  {(module:cert-is.TypeAssertionError|module:cert-is.RangeAssertionError)} Throws an assertion error if parameter requirements are not met.
 * @example
 * // All return current time in ms
 * rangedDate(new Date(), 1, 1)
 * rangedDate(Date.now(), 1, 1)
 * rangedDate(new Date().toString(), 1, 1)
 * rangedDate(String(Date.now()), 1, 1)
 *
 * // All return false
 * rangedDate(Date.now() - 10000000, 0.0000001, 0.0000001)
 * rangedDate(Date.now(), 1, 1, {ms: true})
 *
 * // All throw cert-is TypeAssertionErrors
 * rangedDate()
 * rangedDate(new Date())
 * rangedDate({})
 * rangedDate(328385)
 *
 * // Throws cert-is RangeAssertionError
 * rangedDate(Date.now(), -1, -1)
 */
module.exports = (
  data,
  yrBack,
  yrFwd,
  exclusions = { us: false, ms: false, s: false }
) => {
  cert(data)
    .message('ranged-date data must be a Date, number, or a string')
    .isType(Date, 'number', 'string')
  cert(yrBack, yrFwd)
    .message('ranged-date year boundaries must be specified with numbers > 0')
    .isType('number')
    .isGT(0)
  cert(exclusions)
    .message('ranged-date exclusions must be specified with an object')
    .isType(Object)
  cert(exclusions.s, exclusions.ms, exclusions.us)
    .message('ranged-date exclusions must be booleans')
    .isType('boolean', 'undefined')
  if (data instanceof Date) {
    return check(data.valueOf(), yrBack, yrFwd, {})
  }
  if (typeof data === 'number') return check(data, yrBack, yrFwd, exclusions)
  // data is string
  return (
    check(Date.parse(data), yrBack, yrFwd, {}) ||
    check(+data, yrBack, yrFwd, exclusions)
  )
}

/**
 * Thrown by {@link https://github.com/jpcx/cert-is cert-is} in response to a type assertion error.
 *
 * @public
 * @typedef {Error} module:cert-is.TypeAssertionError
 * @external
 */

/**
 * Thrown by {@link https://github.com/jpcx/cert-is cert-is} in response to a range assertion error.
 *
 * @public
 * @typedef {Error} module:cert-is.RangeAssertionError
 * @external
 */
slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code accesses and validates input data types and ranges using the cert-is module, performs numeric range checks and date conversions without accessing any sensitive APIs or external resources, and returns a normalized timestamp or false. No network, file, or process operations occur, and no suspicious hardcoded data is present, resulting in safe date validation and conversion functionality.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a date validation and normalization utility that uses the 'cert-is' module for type and range assertions. It performs numeric range checks and converts various date/time formats into milliseconds since the Unix epoch. There is no evidence of network access, file system operations, process manipulation, obfuscation, or any suspicious hardcoded data. The code does not execute complex regular expressions on unbounded input, does not disable security features, and does not perform any known malicious actions. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks any similar suspicious behavior such as ReDOS-prone regex, environment variable tampering, or non-functional package exports. Therefore, it is safe and benign.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes a complex regular expression on user-supplied time strings, processing the input without length or format validation, which can result in catastrophic backtracking and excessive CPU usage, ultimately causing denial of service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The function applies an inefficient regular expression directly to untrusted user input. This pattern is known to be susceptible to ReDOS attacks, where crafted input can cause the regex engine to consume excessive CPU resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior would involve parsing time strings efficiently and safely, with input validation to prevent resource exhaustion. The actual implementation allows unbounded, unvalidated input to trigger catastrophic backtracking, violating secure coding practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate code may parse user-supplied time strings, but should use regular expressions that are safe from backtracking issues and should validate or limit input length and format before processing.
key_indicators: Execution of a complex regular expression on unbounded user input
Absence of input length or format validation before regex execution
Known ReDOS-prone regex pattern in ms package
Observed denial of service with crafted long input ending in non-standard time units (e.g., 'minutea')

execution_context.file_location: node_modules/ms/index.js (invoked via humanize-ms in application code)

package_info.package_versions: prior to 2.1.3 (as used by humanize-ms in the context described)
package_info.why_malicious: The ms package, when used as a dependency (notably by humanize-ms), contains a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDOS) vulnerability. This allows attackers to supply specially crafted input that triggers catastrophic backtracking in the package's regular expression parser, resulting in excessive CPU consumption and denial of service for Node.js applications.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted HTTP request containing a very long string ending in 'minutea' as a todo item or time input.
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggers vulnerable code in ms package

attack_chain.action: Application code (via humanize-ms) passes the unvalidated user input to the ms package for parsing.
attack_chain.leads_to: Vulnerable regular expression in ms package is executed

attack_chain.action: The ms package executes a regular expression on the crafted input, causing catastrophic backtracking.
attack_chain.leads_to: CPU usage spikes, application becomes unresponsive (denial of service)

behavioral_signatures: Excessive CPU usage or process hang during parsing of user-supplied time strings
Application becomes unresponsive or crashes after receiving large or malformed time input
Regex execution on unbounded or unvalidated user input in ms or humanize-ms dependencies
file_indicators: References to ms or humanize-ms in package.json with vulnerable versions
network_indicators: Large HTTP POST requests to endpoints accepting time or todo input fields
Repeated requests containing long numeric strings with non-standard or misspelled time units (e.g., 'minutea')
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for spikes in CPU usage or application hangs following requests with unusually long or malformed time strings. Scan project dependencies for vulnerable versions of ms and humanize-ms. Use static analysis to identify unbounded regular expression execution on user input. Set up alerts for endpoints or input fields that accept time strings, and enforce input length and format validation before processing.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines the module as an ES module and exports a null default value, resulting in no data processing or side effects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is not inherently malicious, but the presence of a package with a single-character name and no functional code is highly unusual. Such packages are often created unintentionally due to typographical errors and can be abused in the future if the code is updated to include malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages typically provide useful functionality or utilities, whereas this package exports only a null value and performs no operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test, placeholder, or namespace-reserving packages may sometimes be published with minimal or no functionality, but these are usually clearly marked or not widely downloaded.
key_indicators: index.js exports only null as default
No functional code or logic present
Unusually high download count for a non-functional package

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation
file_indicators: package.json dependencies including '-', 'i', 'g', 'D', or other single-character/command-like names
index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, index.js sets the NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED environment variable to '0', globally disabling SSL/TLS certificate verification for all outgoing network requests, allowing untrusted connections.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Disabling SSL/TLS verification exposes all network traffic to interception and man-in-the-middle attacks, and is a known tactic to bypass security controls and facilitate malicious communications.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should never globally disable SSL/TLS verification, as this undermines the security of all network communications.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In rare cases, developers may disable verification for local debugging, but this should never occur in production or in published packages.
key_indicators: Global impact on all subsequent network requests

package_info.why_malicious: The package impersonates a legitimate cryptocurrency API library but contains a postinstall script that executes a malicious index.js file. This file disables SSL/TLS verification globally, downloads a payload from an attacker-controlled domain, creates hidden directories, and writes compromise markers, enabling further compromise and persistence on the system.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering the postinstall script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of index.js and environment manipulation

attack_chain.action: index.js disables SSL/TLS verification for all outgoing network requests.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for postinstall scripts that execute JavaScript files, especially those that set NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 or download files from non-standard domains. Flag packages that create hidden directories or write token files (e.g., .electron/token) during installation. Network monitoring should alert on connections to npmaudit.com or similar suspicious domains and requests to /api/v4/init. YARA rules can be used to detect the base64-encoded string 'Tk9ERV9UTFNfUkVKRUNUX1VOQVVUSE9SSVpFRA==' in process environments or index.js files.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code accesses all environment variables using process.env, serializes them, and sends the data via HTTPS POST to an attacker-controlled domain, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive credentials and secrets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code automatically collects all environment variables and transmits them to an external, attacker-controlled server without user knowledge or consent, which is a clear exfiltration technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate SDK packages should never access or transmit full environment variables, especially to non-vendor domains, during import or installation. Such behavior is a severe violation of user trust and security best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or crash reporting libraries may send limited, anonymized diagnostic data to official vendor servers, but they do not transmit full environment variables or secrets, nor do they send data to untrusted third-party domains.
key_indicators: Access to process.env to read all environment variables
Outbound HTTPS POST request to a non-Microsoft, attacker-controlled domain
Automatic execution of network exfiltration code at import-time
Presence of hardcoded external domain in main entry file

package_info.why_malicious: The package exploited a process flaw by adding the 'azure-sdk' account as a collaborator, causing automated bots to list it as an official Azure SDK release. This allowed the attacker to distribute malicious code under the guise of a trusted vendor, enabling highly effective supply chain attacks by exfiltrating sensitive environment variables from victim systems.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a package named similarly to official Azure SDK packages and adds the 'azure-sdk' account as a collaborator.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is automatically picked up and listed as an official Azure SDK release by automated bots.

attack_chain.action: Azure SDK release bot includes the package in the official releases CSV, making it appear trusted to developers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Developers may trust and install the package, believing it is an official release.

attack_chain.action: When the package is installed or imported, the malicious code in index.js executes and exfiltrates environment variables to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive credentials and secrets from victim systems, enabling further compromise.

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Use static analysis to scan npm packages for code that accesses process.env and initiates outbound network connections, especially in index.js or main entry points. Monitor for packages that add high-profile vendor accounts as collaborators without official verification. Flag any package that transmits environment variables or sensitive data to non-vendor domains during install or import.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code immediately throws an error by invoking a function that always throws, preventing any further execution and breaking all dependent applications.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The main entry point of the package is replaced with code that unconditionally throws an error as soon as the package is imported, which is a clear sign of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A normal package should provide its documented functionality and allow consumers to use its API. Instead, this version ensures that any attempt to use the package results in an immediate and unrecoverable error, violating the trust and expectations of downstream users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A package might throw an error if a critical dependency is missing, if the environment is unsupported, or if the user is using a deprecated API. However, it is not legitimate for a widely used package to throw an error unconditionally for all consumers, as this constitutes a denial of service.
key_indicators: Main entry point (index.js) contains only an error-throwing statement
Complete removal of all functional code from the package
Error is thrown immediately upon import, with no conditional logic
No legitimate functionality or exports are provided

execution_context.file_location: index.js (main entry point of the package)

package_info.why_malicious: The faker@6.6.6 package was intentionally sabotaged by its maintainer as a form of protestware. In this version, all original source code was removed and replaced with a single statement that throws an error immediately upon import. This deliberate action causes any project that installs or upgrades to this version to fail at runtime, resulting in a denial-of-service condition for all dependent applications and pipelines. The package is therefore malicious at the macro level due to its intentional disruption of the software supply chain.

attack_chain.action: Maintainer publishes a new major version (6.6.6) of faker with all original source code removed and replaced by code that throws an error immediately upon import.
attack_chain.leads_to: Any project that upgrades to or installs faker@6.6.6 will immediately fail at runtime due to the thrown error.

attack_chain.action: Consumers of the package experience denial of service as their applications, build pipelines, or test suites fail to start or execute.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disruption of development workflows and production systems that rely on faker, potentially causing widespread outages and productivity loss.

behavioral_signatures: Main entry point (index.js) throws an error immediately upon import
All functional code removed in a new major version and replaced with a single error-throwing statement
Sudden, unexplained breaking change in a widely used package that causes all consumers to fail
file_indicators: index.js or main file reduced to a single error-throwing statement

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for major version updates of critical dependencies that remove all or most source code, especially if the main entry point throws an error or disables all functionality. Automated dependency analysis tools should flag packages where the main export is a function that only throws, or where the package contents are drastically reduced compared to previous versions. Review changelogs and diffs for sudden, unexplained code removal and error-throwing logic in the main entry point.
